selected.name: Retroactive Reinterpretation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the punchline forces the reader to retroactively reread the setup with an entirely different meaning—the earlier text contained a hidden reading that only becomes visible at the end. Score 0 when the setup's meaning is unchanged by the punchline, or when there is no setup to reinterpret.
selected.rationale: R07's romantic-sounding vows become a Rickroll only in retrospect; R42's 'inconceivable' shifts from emotional to literal. Dense-low R45's flower-petal premise is not retroactively changed by 'I fucked up the flowers,' and R49's 'heard of it' is reinterpreted but predictably and without surprise.

selected.name: Platform in-group meta-humor about the joke's own reception
selected.instruction: Score whether the joke explicitly references the posting/voting mechanics of the forum itself (reposts, karma, upvotes, front page, comments) as part of its content, and whether that reference is turned into an actual joke rather than a literal complaint. A 10 uses forum-mechanics content as the vehicle for a genuine ironic or self-aware punchline. A 0 either has no forum-mechanics content, or mentions it only as a flat, un-twisted complaint/disclaimer.
selected.rationale: R42 ('This joke won't get any upvotes...') and R52 (the Reddit-addiction dialogue) turn platform mechanics into a self-aware punchline and are dense_high_card_low, while R08 (flat repost complaint, duplicated text) and R14 ('make sure I know this is a repost') use the same subject matter as a literal, un-twisted disclaimer and are dense_low_card_high -- the contrast suggests the scorecard may be crediting the topic of platform-meta-commentary regardless of whether it's actually turned into a joke.
member_names: Forum-complaint content with no independent joke

Platform in-group meta-humor about the joke's own reception

selected.name: Transgression carried by a mechanism, not by shock alone
selected.instruction: Composite, for items with taboo, offensive, dark, or sexual content. Score whether a formal comic mechanism (pun, reversal, misdirection, unexpected literalism) does the work. 10 = the transgressive material is the vehicle for a real mechanism that would still be a joke shape if the topic were tame. 5 = a mechanism is present but thin, and the taboo is doing most of the lifting. 0 = the item states something transgressive with no mechanism at all -- the offence IS the content. Items with no transgressive content are not applicable and should score 5.
selected.rationale: R59 and R38 run real reversals through their transgression and are dense-high; R04 and R26 assert something transgressive flat, with no pivot, and are dense-bottom while the scorecard rates R26 at .998. A bank criterion for 'edginess' or 'boldness' cannot tell these apart.
member_names: Taboo content routed through misdirection vs. stated flatly

selected.name: Reads as freshly minted rather than a circulated chestnut
selected.instruction: Score how much the item reads as a joke the writer constructed versus a standard that has been in circulation for decades and is reproduced here verbatim. 10 = the premise, the pivot and the phrasing all feel newly assembled; a well-read judge does not recognise it. 5 = a familiar frame with a new payload, or a new frame with a familiar payload. 0 = a canonical chestnut whose punchline the judge could recite before reaching it, transcribed with no alteration. Judge only recognisability and staleness of the material as text; do not consider how the item might be received.
selected.rationale: The scorecard-high side is dense with museum pieces: R13 is the 'dancing with your honey... it's snot' rhyme, R14 is the two-aerials-married-great-ceremony-terrible-reception standard, R09 is 'put it on the record', R23 is the supercalifragilistic Gandhi construction, and R45 is the 'I'm a Believer' bit. Their card percentiles run .653-.992 while dense sits at .096-.462. Every one of these is well-formed, symmetrical, and clean, so a bank of written craft criteria will score them near the top; a reader tracking whether an audience finds the item funny is instead tracking whether it has been seen before. This is the most likely single explanation for the entire dense-low / card-high half of the slice.
member_names: Phrasing and template are not stock
Reads as freshly minted rather than a circulated chestnut

selected.name: Topical/political specificity
selected.instruction: Score how much the joke's humor depends on knowledge of a specific, named contemporary political figure or news event (as opposed to being evergreen). A 10 is entirely dependent on current political personalities/events for its meaning. A 0 has no political content and would read identically in any decade.
selected.rationale: R40 (Monica Lewinsky/Bernie/Clinton), R45 (Hillary Clinton email AMA), R47 (White House 'garbage'), and R48 (Obama/ISIL naming) are all explicitly tied to a specific political news cycle and cluster in the dense_low_card_high half of the slice, suggesting the scorecard may be crediting topical political references that the dense model discounts as not inherently funny.
member_names: Dependence on a news-cycle figure or event
Reference is structural and durable rather than pegged to a news beat

selected.name: Pop Culture or Lyric Bait-and-Switch
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the joke uses a conversational tone to seamlessly disguise a famous movie quote, trope, or song lyric until the very end; score 0 if there is no disguised pop culture reference.
selected.rationale: The dense model highly rates clever lyric or quote integration (R27, R55), a stylistic device the scorecard fails to credit because it may look like a standard non-sequitur.

selected.name: Narrative timing and final turn
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sequence of beats, dialogue, or pauses builds expectation and lands a well-timed final turn; score 0 when additional lines do not develop or improve the punch.
selected.rationale: R08, R21, R27, R34, and R47 use staged narration or dialogue, while their varied quality suggests that timing and beat structure deserve separate attention from mere length.

selected.name: Clean semantic double-use
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a key word or phrase naturally supports both the setup meaning and a distinct punchline meaning; score 0 when there is no double meaning or the connection is forced.
selected.rationale: R01, R03, R05, R18, R24, and R56 all hinge on a word carrying two compatible readings, but their disagreement suggests this mechanism is not consistently captured.

selected.name: Setup is a complete, self-standing situation
selected.instruction: Score whether the setup gives the reader a coherent, complete scenario before the punch arrives. 10 = a reader can state exactly what situation is being described. 5 = the situation is inferable but requires a re-read or a charitable guess. 0 = the setup is a fragment, is cut off, has no clear subject or referent, or is so garbled that the reader cannot say what is being described.
selected.rationale: R60 stops mid-setup ('So, once I had that conversation:') and R10 is syntactically unresolvable, yet both draw .59-.63 from the scorecard while sitting at dense .069 and .063. R06's dialogue leaves it unclear who is confused about what. Contrast R15 and R44, which establish a fully specified situation and run dense-high.
member_names: Both readings independently licensed by the setup
Both senses of the pivot phrase hold fully in context
Setup is a complete, self-standing situation

selected.name: Distinctive comic persona
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the narrator or character exhibits a specific, recognizable attitude or behavior that generates humor; score 0 when the joke has no discernible persona beyond stating information.
selected.rationale: The schemes and attitudes in R19, R22, R34, R42, and R60 make character perspective central rather than incidental.

selected.name: Cross-domain collision
selected.instruction: Score 10 when two normally unrelated knowledge domains intersect through one coherent comic hinge; score 0 when the domains are routine, disconnected, or never meaningfully combined.
selected.rationale: R21 combines mathematics with moral symbolism, R25 combines scripture with forum culture, and R52 combines measurement, religion, and disaster terminology.

selected.name: Nerdy or Academic Wordplay
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the punchline explicitly requires knowledge of STEM, math, grammar, or specific academic trivia to understand; score 0 if the joke requires no specialized academic knowledge.
selected.rationale: The dense model heavily rewards niche, nerdy humor (R48, R51, R57), whereas the scorecard undervalues this specific subculture, likely penalizing the required cognitive leap.

selected.name: Natural phonetic transformation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sound-alike smoothly transforms a familiar phrase into the punchline; score 0 when pronunciation or spelling makes the connection strained.
selected.rationale: R06, R22, and R35 use compact sound-based transformations, whereas R28 and R56 show how phonetic material can become awkward or overextended.

selected.name: Novelty of Pun vs Cliché
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the wordplay feels highly original, fresh, and specific to the context; score 0 if the pun is a widely known, ancient cliché (e.g., super-calloused mystics, or terrible aerial reception).
selected.rationale: The scorecard overvalues archaic, well-known puns simply for having a pun structure (R04, R59), whereas the dense model appreciates fresher, more novel wordplay (R51, R55).

selected.name: Wordplay anchored to a specific named entity
selected.instruction: Score how tightly the joke's pun/wordplay is built around a specific proper noun (a celebrity, brand, title, or franchise name) such that the joke would not work if the name were swapped out. A 10 depends entirely on the specific named entity's sound, spelling, or public identity for the punchline. A 0 uses no proper noun or could substitute any name without changing the joke.
selected.rationale: R17 turns on 'Princess Buttercup and Wesley' from The Princess Bride to land 'inconceivable,' R56 depends on the specific Monkees lyric 'I'm a Believer... then I saw her face,' and R33 and R37 hinge on 'turntable/record' and 'Macbeth.docx' respectively -- all are cases of tight name-anchored wordplay spanning both disagreement directions, suggesting it's a distinguishable craft dimension worth scoring on its own.
member_names: Wordplay anchored to a specific named entity

selected.name: Datable topical reference fixing the item to one forum era
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item is pinned to a specific period by its references: named politicians or public figures in a time-bound role, live news events, election or scandal references, calendar markers ('end of the decade'), platform or technology idiom belonging to one era, and slang whose currency was time-limited. 0 = fully timeless, could have been written in any decade; 4 = one dated reference that is incidental; 7 = the setup depends on a situation that was current only for a period; 10 = the item is unintelligible without knowing a specific news cycle. Score how narrowly the text can be dated, not how old it seems. The judge MUST NOT judge whether the reference is stale, fresh, or well-chosen, and MUST NOT judge the politics involved -- only how tightly the text localises itself in time.
selected.rationale: Mode-3 position-in-container channel: I cannot see the post date, so I score the era fingerprint the date leaves in the text. This is a pure nuisance -- the era an item was posted in changes the comparison pool and the audience's appetite without changing the joke's construction. The slice is strongly stratified by era: R28 (Hillary Clinton's emails), R38 (Obama and ISIL), R59 (Monica Lewinsky voting for Bernie), R33 (Bruce Jenner's transition), R27 ('before the end of the decade') and R40 (White House garbage rally) are all datable and all dense-low/card-high, while R05 ('Please hurry up with Trump') is the datable outlier on the dense-high/card-low side. R31's Toby-Maguire-Spiderman framing dates it the same way through pop culture rather than politics.

selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of visible spelling errors, malformed grammar, inconsistent capitalization, or title-body mismatches. Judge only the textual presence of these features; do not judge whether they are good, funny, or effective.
selected.rationale: Proofreading or posting haste can leave a recognizable trace without measuring humor. Examples include the misspellings in R06, R11, and R22.

selected.name: Forum/Platform Meta-Reference
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the text explicitly mentions the platform, its voting mechanisms (e.g., upvotes, front page), or its own status as a post/repost. Do not judge if this makes the text good or bad.
selected.rationale: Mentioning the forum mechanics is a stylistic marker of a post tailored to the venue rather than a standalone joke. R22 ('This joke won't get any upvotes'), R28 ('technically a repost'), and R41 ('why I never post jokes on this sub') rely heavily on this meta-commentary.

selected.name: Repost/retelling-chain acknowledgment
selected.instruction: 0-10: how explicitly does the text mark itself as a retelling, repost, or repetition of a joke that has circulated before (e.g., 'technically a repost', 'make sure I know this is a repost', 'reposting because', or the item's own text literally repeating itself). 0 = presents as wholly original/new; 10 = explicitly and prominently flags itself as a repeat/repost. Score only the presence of this self-marking, not whether the retelling is skillful.
selected.rationale: R31 ('This joke is technically a repost, but I didn't see it anywhere on reddit...'), R59 ('make sure I know this is a repost'), and R56 (whose entire text is literally duplicated, itself joking about reposts reaching the front page) all textually flag a position in a retelling chain, which can shift crowd reception via repost fatigue or nostalgia apart from joke quality -- though genuine staying power can also be why a joke keeps recirculating.

selected.name: Taboo-register salience
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of shock, slur-adjacency, sexual, scatological, death-related, religious, or otherwise taboo subject matter. Judge only register intensity; do not judge whether the material is funny, acceptable, or well handled.
selected.rationale: Taboo material can act as a circulation and attention channel distinct from craft. Examples include death and terrorism in R07, sexual content in R32, and slur-adjacent wording in R31 and R58.

selected.name: Audience-management furniture: apologies, disclaimers, permission-seeking
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of furniture addressed to the reader that sits outside the joke proper: apologies or pre-emptive excuses ('sorry if repost', 'I know, I'm a terrible person'), disclaimers and content warnings, edit notes, first-post announcements, solidarity bids ('I can't be the only one'), requests or predictions about reception phrased as address to the audience, and hedges about the item's own originality. 0 = the item is joke text only, with no line spoken to the reader about the post itself; 5 = one clause of such furniture; 10 = half or more of the item is this furniture. Count words of furniture relative to total words. The judge MUST NOT judge whether the furniture is charming, annoying, or well-written, and MUST NOT infer anything about the poster's character -- score only how much furniture is physically present in the text.
selected.rationale: This is Mode-2/Mode-4 furniture: it is a trace of the unseen poster's standing and nerves, not of the joke's engineering, but a practised poster who omits it may also write tighter jokes, so mixed=true. R17 ('This joke is technically a repost, but I didn't see it anywhere on reddit so I thought I might add it. I know, I'm a terrible person.') is almost entirely furniture and lands dense-high/card-low; R15 is furniture masquerading as the whole joke and lands dense-low/card-high; R12 ('I can't be the only one who...') is the solidarity-bid variant, also dense-low/card-high. Three rows, three different placements on the disagreement axis -- the furniture is doing work in the models that is separable from the punch.
member_names: Audience-management furniture: apologies, disclaimers, repost notes

selected.name: Taboo and shock loading as a circulation register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item leans on taboo material: explicit sexual or scatological content, slurs or slur-adjacent ethnic/religious/national targeting, disability or transgender targeting, atrocity and mass-death references, death of a named or implied real person, and violence played for effect. 0 = no taboo content of any kind; 3 = a mild off-colour word with no target; 6 = the taboo element is present and named but the punch does not depend on it; 10 = the punch is the taboo itself, with nothing left if the taboo material is removed. Score intensity and centrality of taboo content. The judge MUST NOT judge whether the item is offensive, acceptable, brave, lazy, or funny, and MUST NOT apply any moral evaluation -- this is a content-inventory score only.
selected.rationale: Mode-4 register-of-taboo channel. It is predictive because shock loading drives attention independently of construction, but it is not a quality signal in either direction -- taboo jokes span the full craft range -- and because a shock premise can also be genuinely well-built, mixed=true. The slice carries a heavy taboo load on both sides of the disagreement, which is precisely why it must be declared: R49 (Eid on 9/11, 'gonna be the bomb') and R50 (9/11 dead-father joke) are dense-low/card-high, as are R54 (N-word/F-word) and R58 (anal/'butt fuck it'); meanwhile R25 (bucket-of-shit vs a Roma slur), R43 ('Muslim Barbie... blow-up doll') and R44 ('Adam and Eve not Adam and Steve') are dense-high/card-low. Same register, opposite disagreement sign -- a textbook nuisance to discount both models against.

selected.name: Delivery-template commitment
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how strongly the item commits to a recognizable delivery template such as a one-liner, riddle, dialogue, narrative, list, or lyric parody. Judge only structural commitment, not whether the format works well.
selected.rationale: Posters and communities often favor recurring delivery templates, which can be predictive as a format signal without being a humor judgment. R01 and R50 use dialogue templates, while R55 uses an extended narrative build.
